q: A patient with an FEV1 of 70% predicted is listed for right lower lobectomy (5 of 19 segments). What is the predicted post-operative (ppo) FEV1?
why: ppo value = pre-op value × (19 − segments resected) / 19 = 70 × 14/19 ≈ 52%.

q: Under BTS guidance, which ppoFEV1 or ppoDLCO is acceptable for lobectomy without further testing?
why: A ppoFEV1 or ppoDLCO above 40% is acceptable (there is no separate higher threshold for pneumonectomy). Lower values need exercise testing (shuttle walk, stair climb, CPET) and MDT discussion.

q: Which pneumonectomy carries the higher risk of post-pneumonectomy pulmonary oedema, and what is its mortality?
why: Post-pneumonectomy pulmonary oedema is more common after right pneumonectomy and carries a mortality of over 50%. Restrictive fluids are part of prevention.

q: A patient with a large bronchopleural fistula needs ventilation. Which strategy is most appropriate?
o: Volume control with high tidal volumes
High PEEP to splint the fistula
Spontaneous ventilation where possible; otherwise pressure control, low tidal volume and low PEEP
why: Favour spontaneous ventilation; if PPV is needed use pressure control, low tidal volume, low PEEP, permissive hypercapnia, a lower SpO2 target and a short inspiratory time to reduce leak.

q: During one-lung ventilation for lobectomy, SpO2 falls to 85%. What should you do first?
o: Apply CPAP to the non-ventilated lung
Increase FiO2 to 1.0, tell the team and call for help
Start two-lung ventilation for the rest of the case
why: Step 1 is FiO2 1.0, alert the team and get help. Then confirm tube position with the bronchoscope, recruit and add PEEP to the ventilated lung, CPAP to the non-ventilated lung, then intermittent two-lung ventilation.

q: Which technique is generally the first choice for analgesia after VATS lobectomy?
o: Intercostal blocks at a single level
why: A paravertebral block is generally first choice for thoracic surgery; it needs an intact pleura. An erector spinae catheter is an alternative, and epidural is used for open surgery.

q: After thoracotomy with a working paravertebral catheter, the patient complains of ipsilateral shoulder pain. What is the likely cause?
why: Shoulder pain is referred via the phrenic nerve from pleural or diaphragmatic irritation, which a paravertebral block does not cover. Treat with NSAIDs and paracetamol, withdraw the drain slightly, or consider a phrenic nerve block.

q: Which arrhythmia accounts for most of the arrhythmias seen after pneumonectomy?
why: Arrhythmias occur in about 60% after pneumonectomy (30–50% after lung resection overall), and 60–70% of them are AF.

q: For a patient with severe COPD, endobronchial valves are being considered instead of lung volume reduction surgery. Which finding makes valves ineffective?
why: Endobronchial valves let air out but not in; they fail if collateral ventilation refills the target lobe.

q: By what main mechanism does lung volume reduction surgery improve symptoms in severe COPD?
o: It increases surface area for gas exchange
It reduces dynamic hyperinflation and increases elastic recoil of the remaining lung
why: LVRS is palliative: it reduces dynamic hyperinflation and improves the elastic recoil of the remaining lung.
